claims.claim_text: Surplus processor headroom in a flight controller is spent partly on running a real-time operating system, because preemptive time scheduling removes the risk that adding a feature slows down or disturbs the features already present.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of that time scheduling stuff and the preemptive stuff gets easier and you don't worry about collisions and, you know, adding a feature that ends up slowing down or messing up other features
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: When streaming acquisition data to a desktop machine, the limiting factor is not peak bandwidth but latency: a general-purpose operating system is not real-time and will periodically go off and do something else, so the design question becomes sustained bandwidth and how large a buffer is needed at each end to cover the gaps.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not a real-time operating system. It's the – you know, the peak bandwidth is fine. It's the sustained bandwidth and how big a buffer you need at each end to cover the gaps.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: A full Linux system is not deterministic, so pulling networking work onto the main processor of an embedded design leads either to an RTOS or to accepting non-deterministic timing; the alternative is a module with its own dedicated processor for the stack.
claims.quote_verbatim: If it's full-blown Linux, then it's a real operating system, right? It's not deterministic at that point.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: One practitioner position, from an author of an embedded systems book that deliberately omits the topic, is to remove an RTOS wherever possible and use either bare metal or a small scheduler with message passing instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I have my choice, I will rip out any RTOS. I mean, my book actually doesn't cover an RTOS at all because I prefer to go bare metal or with a little dinky scheduler message passer
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: In robotics and in audio and visual effect systems, which must respond quickly, the latency an RTOS introduces can be judged not worth its benefits; where one is used, the developer has to stay aware of what the scheduler is doing at any moment.
claims.quote_verbatim: We don't have an RTOS because the RTOS's latency just isn't worth it to us.
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Early mobile robot control was built on VME-bus single-board computers running Wind River Systems' VxWorks real-time operating system, with a tether back to a VAX in the laboratory carrying the high-level control.
claims.quote_verbatim: the VME computer was running Wind River Systems VXWorks real-time operating system
claims.speaker: Gerry Roston
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Gerry Roston

claims.claim_text: A fixed time-slice scheduler wastes the remainder of any slice a task finishes early, whereas an RTOS scheduler does not wait for the slice to expire and moves immediately to the next task.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because it doesn't wait for the one 512th. It just goes to the next thing.
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Espressif's ESP-IDF, the SDK for the ESP32, is built around an RTOS port that was extended to run multi-core, and that kernel forms the base of the whole SDK.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like in the original RTOS implementation for that port it did to be multi-core. And now, um, yeah, it's essentially the base of the SDK we have.
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeroen Domburg (Sprite_tm)

claims.claim_text: Repeated surveys of embedded developers found that a large fraction of projects, in the range of forty to fifty percent, ran a homegrown real-time operating system rather than a third-party or open-source one, making the custom RTOS the single most common kind in use.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was a significant chunk, like 40 to 50% were homegrown
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Alternate Info Sources

claims.claim_text: Writing an in-house RTOS is straightforward at the outset; the cost appears in continuing support years later, and in the fact that every subsequent addition must be integrated into a private code base rather than taken from a shared ecosystem.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not, it's not the beginning that's hard. It's the continuing support four years down the line. That's the hard part.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Alternate Info Sources

claims.claim_text: Running an RTOS does not by itself make a design low power; consumption is determined by whether the system actually enters sleep, and treating the operating system as a substitute for deliberate power management is a mistake.
claims.quote_verbatim: He's like, well, what, what about that makes it low power? And I was like, yeah, yeah, no, it's a good point.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Sipping Coulombs

claims.claim_text: The Rabbit 2000 used a CPU architecture of its own design, similar to but written from scratch against the Z80, and shipped with an integrated real-time C operating system simple enough that a developer with no RTOS background could implement a properly scheduled system with it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it came with its own real time C operating system, which was so easy to use. Even a dummy like me could implement a real time operating system
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Feels over reals

claims.claim_text: Real-time operating systems were historically third-party products bought under licence for thousands of dollars per seat; mature open-source kernels aimed at connected devices later removed that cost from the decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you wanted one, you bought one, right. And it costs thousands of dollars to buy a license for this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Feels over reals

claims.claim_text: The Rabbit 2000 carried four UARTs at a time when no microcontroller on the market offered that many, and its real-time operating system was integrated directly with the C compiler so that the scheduling calls were part of the supplied toolchain.
claims.quote_verbatim: it had really nice real-time operating system integration with the C compiler
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Keyzermas All The Way

claims.claim_text: Porting an existing motion-control project to a multi-core RTOS-based part was made harder by documentation written at the level of introductory sketches: the public API functions were listed, but what is safe to call from an interrupt, what works under the RTOS and what does not, and the behaviour behind the API were undocumented.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of the things that aren't documented are what works in interrupts, what works in the RTOS, what doesn't
claims.speaker: Bart Dring
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Servicing web requests on the same processor as step generation produced visible stutter in motion under high network traffic, because the network work interrupted a step in progress; the resolution was to confine the motion code to one core with a single primary thread plus interrupts and avoid the RTOS there, even though the vendor API expects RTOS use throughout.
claims.quote_verbatim: by using the one core and avoiding the RTOS for Gerbil, I was using, um, just a primary thread and interrupts. Um, and, um, but the API is very RTOS friendly.
claims.speaker: Bart Dring
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Splitting a design across a Linux core, a bare-metal or RTOS core and custom logic in FPGA fabric spends timing budget on every crossing between them, and forces decisions about buffer size, how often the Linux side services the interface, and what happens to accumulated data when a service call does not arrive.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you got to consider like what your buffer size is, like how frequency is Linux serving this servicing this thing? What happens if like that call never comes, you know, you're stuck with all this data you got to dump.
claims.speaker: Ryan Cousins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: Real-time operating systems are individually not difficult to use; the recurring cost is that each one is different, so changing kernel means learning an entirely new API.
claims.quote_verbatim: The problem is that every single one is different. You've got to learn a whole new API every time you change RTOSs.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: As Wind River's attention moved toward embedded Linux and larger embedded processing, the volume share of the microcontroller RTOS space passed to free kernels such as FreeRTOS.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I look at who's winning in the RTOS space, it's things like FreeRTOS
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Each task in an RTOS is given its own stack, so the memory budget of an RTOS-based design scales with the number of tasks rather than with a single call depth.
claims.quote_verbatim: each task has its own stack
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Knob and Tube Wiring

claims.claim_text: Ownership of the major microcontroller kernels has consolidated into large software companies, with FreeRTOS held by Amazon and ThreadX by Microsoft, while Zephyr is stewarded by the Linux Foundation.
claims.quote_verbatim: Amazon's got free, owns free RTOS. Microsoft owns thread.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fear of Banjos

claims.claim_text: The standing objections to adopting an RTOS are that it consumes processor time, that it adds complexity, and that it requires dynamic memory allocation — the last of which is untrue in many cases.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to slow your processor down. You're using up time. You know, it's overly complex. Like, you need to use dynamic memory allocation, which is not true in a lot of cases.
claims.speaker: Eli Hughes
claims.episode_title: Brewing Electronics with Eli Hughes

claims.claim_text: For tightly written signal-processing code in which every sample that arrives is processed and passed straight out, a superloop with a handful of functions carries no scheduling overhead and an RTOS adds nothing the application needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of my applications were really, really tight DSP code and things that it was so simple not to have the overhead
claims.speaker: Eli Hughes
claims.episode_title: Brewing Electronics with Eli Hughes

claims.claim_text: Much of what modern embedded frameworks provide is a cross-hardware abstraction layer rather than real-time behaviour; the part that properly belongs to the RTOS is the kernel itself — the scheduling of threads and the primitives such as semaphores that coordinate them.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a cross hardware platform extraction, abstraction layer.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Focus, Dammit

claims.claim_text: An RTOS on a microcontroller remains the right answer for appliance-class products: a controller with an LCD, a heater, a stirring pump and a temperature sensor is comfortably within microcontroller reach, and the presence of a touchscreen does not by itself imply a Linux-class system.
claims.quote_verbatim: as soon as you have a touchscreen, it doesn't mean, oh, you need to run Linux
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson
claims.episode_title: Embedded Linux with Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: Graphical toolkits are a real deciding factor between a microcontroller RTOS and embedded Linux: the free embedded GUI libraries are workable but unattractive and awkward, while the commercial ones that look and perform well cost on the order of ten thousand dollars in licence fees, which matters most on low-volume products.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going to pay 10 K for a license
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson
claims.episode_title: Embedded Linux with Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: A power-conversion product can express its scheduling entirely in interrupt priorities: interrupts at one kilohertz, one hundred hertz and ten hertz handle different work with the faster ones prioritised, and a thirty-seven kilohertz interrupt in the power module must always be served. Where that structure already meets the requirement, adding an RTOS offers no immediate benefit.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if you're going to put it in our R2OS, I don't see the immediate benefit for us. Maybe we can get it to work, but if we don't need it, why go for it?
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: In an interrupt-driven power controller, data crosses between interrupt levels through global variables: a set point arriving over CAN or an analogue input is stored in a global, and the thirty-seven kilohertz interrupt reads the latest value when it fires.
claims.quote_verbatim: So when the 37 kilohertz interrupt fires off, it has the latest value in some global variable that it will just read.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: An alternative to reconciling hard timing with communications in one scheduler is to split them across processors: dedicate a core or a programmable real-time unit, such as those on TI parts, to the critical switching task, and run Linux or an RTOS on another core for the less critical communications work.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe I could use the PRUs to do the switching of the IGBTs and then I can use run Linux or something on the other one
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: FreeRTOS carries no IP stack and no concept of networking, because it was created at a time when most RTOS-based products were unconnected devices such as medical instruments and Bluetooth headsets; kernels of a later generation were designed with internet connectivity as an integral part.
claims.quote_verbatim: free RTOS doesn't have an IP stack, doesn't have even a concept of networking
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: For most connected products the real-time property of an RTOS is the least consequential thing it provides, which is why practitioners have argued the category is misnamed.
claims.quote_verbatim: used to hate the term RTOS. And he's like, yeah, the real time part is the most inconsequential aspect
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: What such systems mostly deliver is a hardware or platform abstraction layer: the application programs against a UART object rather than device registers, and against a network connection object rather than a raw TCP/IP stack.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of registers, it's you arts, um, or instead of TCP IP, it's, you know, this TCP library network dot connector
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: Moving from a single-vendor SDK to a cross-vendor RTOS trades a well-defined toolchain, where a specific debug probe and IDE could be assumed and searched for online, for a Linux-like model of assembling existing pieces, which brings its own learning cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's kind of almost close to the Linux where you're kind of patching stuff together versus necessarily writing a whole bunch of custom things
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Creative Engineering with Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: An RTOS should be treated like any other dependency and wrapped behind an interface the project controls — a mutex lock and unlock taking a handle, rather than direct calls to the kernel API — so the same application code can be built and tested on a development machine as well as on the target.
claims.quote_verbatim: treat it like any other dependency. So, you know, you want to interact with an interface that sits on top of the RTOS that you control, because then now I'm in a better position to swap out my code so it can run on my development machine for tests versus on the RTOS
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: Adopting an RTOS moves work forward into design: thread priorities, the threaded architecture as a whole, and the possibility of deadlock or priority inversion all become decisions that must be made deliberately rather than emerging from the code.
claims.quote_verbatim: how do I set thread priorities? You know, what is my threaded architecture? Am I going to have deadlocks? You know, or a priority inversion.
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: Engineers who have been programming embedded systems for years frequently do not know what an RTOS is or why they would want one; the question they arrive with is what they need beyond a C compiler.
claims.quote_verbatim: inevitably they don't really know what an RTOS is, or why they would want to use one
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: The first question before adopting an RTOS is whether a state machine would meet the requirement: for a genuinely small system it is the better option.
claims.quote_verbatim: well, would a state machine do what you're really needing? It's like, if so, and it's really small, that might be the best option
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: The decision is easier on a clean-sheet project than on inherited code, because knowing the minimum requirements up front, and which features are merely desirable after the first working version, bounds the problem well enough to choose an architecture.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you know ahead of time, minimum requirements and then desirements after, you know, that, that MVP is done, then you can usually get a pretty good idea
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: The reliable indicators that a design wants an RTOS are a user interface, particularly an on-board graphical one, and extensive communications capability — network connectivity, USB, or heavy use of SPI and UART.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have a user interface, almost definitely because, you know, especially like a GUI and onboard GUI or something like that. Anything with extensive communications capability for sure.
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: FreeRTOS and most microcontroller-targeted kernels are essentially only a scheduler plus basic primitives — queues, semaphores and task notifications — with no libraries or drivers supplied, which is the substantive difference from a full operating system such as Linux where libraries and drivers come with the system.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's pretty much just a scheduler and like some really basic things like, you know, cues, semaphores, task notifications, that kind of stuff. So there isn't, you don't have any libraries
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: A high-priority critical task must not wait on resources shared with lower-priority work: blocking on a mutex guarding a large block of shared memory stalls the task that has the deadline. The critical task should run continuously and push its results out to the rest of the system through a queue.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want to get into a situation where there's this crazy big block of shared memory and you're waiting on a mutex for something to update. You know, you just want that, you want that critical task to be continuously running.
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: A periodic task under an RTOS does not busy-wait for its interval: it declares that it is sleeping for the period, which returns the processor to the scheduler for other work. Tasks are usually partitioned by group of responsibilities rather than made extremely fine-grained.
claims.quote_verbatim: instead of saying like, wait 5,000 milliseconds, it says, I'm going to go to sleep for 5,000 milliseconds
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: Interrupt priorities should be configured so that the scheduler's own interrupt sits below every critical interrupt; the critical handler reads the streaming sensor data unconditionally, stores it away, and posts a semaphore once enough has accumulated, at which point the scheduler runs the tasks that consume it.
claims.quote_verbatim: so that your scheduler interrupt is a lower priority than any of your critical interrupts
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: Because an RTOS supplies task scheduling it is tempting to stop using hardware interrupts altogether; that is possible to program but requires great care, since the timing guarantees of a hardware interrupt are not the same as those of a scheduled task.
claims.quote_verbatim: you actually don't ever need to use an actual hardware interrupt anymore because basically an interrupt is built in. You have to be careful there. You have to be very, very careful there.
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: The point at which a program outgrows a superloop is recognisable in its structure: a long-running computation has to be interrupted repeatedly to check unrelated conditions, such as whether a buffer is overflowing, so those checks end up sprinkled through the routine.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have some routine that's chugging through a complex math calculation or whatever. Right. And in the middle of that, you need to check to see if your, your buffer is overflowing or whatever. So you wind up with all these reads, these unrelated things sprinkled throughout.
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: An RTOS can be instrumented so that timing itself is observable: record when each task was activated, how long it ran, and whether it overran its real-time constraint. The data can be emitted as a continuous stream or reduced to statistics — minimum, maximum and average runtime plus a counter of missed deadlines — which is what makes timing defects visible during implementation and test.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can instrument when a task was activated, how long it ran, did it like overrun it, it's constraint, it's real time constraint.
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Reducing task timing to running statistics rather than a full trace keeps the instrumentation affordable: minimum, maximum and average runtime with a missed-deadline count carries most of the diagnostic value of a per-activation stream.
claims.quote_verbatim: So minimum runtime, maximum runtime, average runtime, and then like a counter for the number of times you miss the deadline.
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: A system is real-time when a result it depends on — a sensor reading or a computation — must be available within a bounded time, and its absence within that bound constitutes a failure rather than merely a delay.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you are relying on a result from something, whether that's reading a sensor or computation, that result has to be available within a certain amount of time, or there's a failure
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Before writing code, the classes of problem present in a system should be identified explicitly — for example distributed-system problems and real-time problems — because each is an established field of study whose literature has to be worked through rather than rediscovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: before you start writing any code or designing anything, figure out what class of problems you have
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Much of what an RTOS supplies looks self-evidently useful — assigning priorities to button presses and to screen updates so that the display always refreshes — but on human timescales the difference between a thirty and a two hundred millisecond response is immaterial, so those requirements alone do not justify one.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have these events, like generally speaking, I have, you know, some event driven system and button pushes, you know, have a certain priority and updating the screen as a certain priority
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: An RTOS is not free: code must be structured for it and the developer must understand how the kernel will execute that code. If the guiding principle is keeping the state space small enough for one person, or at least the team, to hold in mind, the threshold for adding an RTOS rises accordingly.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is sort of like, you know, some complexity with structuring or code for a real time operating system and knowing how the real time operating system is going to execute that code
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: In a hub-and-spoke system the peripheral nodes and end effectors need not run a real-time operating system themselves; concentrating it in the central computer keeps the number of RTOS-based images to be maintained down as spokes are added.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe those sort of nodes on the, on the periphery, the actual end effectors, the end nodes doesn't necessarily need to run a real-time operating system
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Much RTOS-like behaviour is available without a task-switching kernel: a conventional superloop can set flags as events arrive and then test those flags in the intended priority order, or queue the events and service the queue, which is adequate wherever the processor has enough headroom that timing is not tight.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have a standard super loop. And when events come in, you're setting flags. And then you just check those flags in the priority order that you want to get them done.
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Sensors requiring very tight timing can be handled by a microcontroller with a real-time operating system, but only a fairly powerful one; FPGAs and CPLDs suit that combination of tight timing and parallel processing more naturally.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe you could do it with a micro controller and a real time operating system, but you probably need quite a beefy one
claims.speaker: Leigh Brady
claims.episode_title: Siloed Engineering with Leigh Brady

claims.claim_text: Working on an RTOS-based system without step debugging leaves the developer inferring behaviour from print messages and assuming the rest is working; getting a debugger attached and stepping code is the point at which that guesswork stops.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't have any like debugging capabilities in like an, in a real-time operating system. It was kind of just like, well, everything's probably going okay because I can, you know, I see a print message
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mute Button Discipline

claims.claim_text: A connected sensor card was built on an STM32L4R5, a part with 640 kB of RAM and 2 MB of flash running a simple RTOS, after mocking the system up at a high level on a Raspberry Pi or BeagleBone first.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's 640 K of RAM. It's two megabytes, megabytes of flash of storage, a little simple RTOS.
claims.speaker: Ray Ozzie
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ray Ozzie (Blues Wireless)

claims.claim_text: Under an RTOS, work that would conventionally require a hardware timer — tracking a rotary encoder or a beam interrupter, for example — can be done with kernel timing services instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: You really don't need hardware timers when you have a real-time operating system
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Robo Fry Guy

claims.claim_text: The substitution of kernel timing for hardware timers holds only within the resolution the scheduler can deliver: intervals in the region of tenths of a second are comfortable, while microsecond timing becomes difficult and belongs back in hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like, it starts to get hard at microseconds, you know, if you're doing sort of like, you know, something in the early second region, you know, it's, you know, it's fine.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Robo Fry Guy

claims.claim_text: A team that had run FreeRTOS for over two years declined to move to Zephyr for two stated reasons: keeping a single kernel across all projects, and the fact that work outside Zephyr's well-trodden domain — ultra-low power on a platform that has not been developed for it — becomes considerably more complex. The corresponding cost of FreeRTOS is that it ships no drivers and each must be written.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you try to do like ultra low power on a platform, that's not been developed or do things different way, it's a lot more complex
claims.speaker: Alvaro Prieto
claims.episode_title: Reunion Impedance Matching and 2023 Predictions

claims.claim_text: A cross-vendor RTOS is technically the same object as any other — a scheduler, threads, queues, semaphores and mutexes — but is adopted mainly for its ecosystem: shared drivers for networking and radio are written centrally while each silicon vendor supplies a compatibility layer, so the same kernel and application code retarget across chipsets.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is a scheduler. There's threads. There's queues and all of the semaphores and mutexes and all the things you read about every time you read about it in RTOS. But that's not really why most people are talking about Zephyr
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Automotive real-time operating systems are built around basic tasks, which run to completion once kicked off on a fixed period such as every ten milliseconds; nearly all real-time processing in a vehicle can be expressed that way.
claims.quote_verbatim: nearly all of your real-time processing can be done with these basic tasks. Uh, they're called basic tasks, the run to completion tasks. So you just kick them off every 10 milliseconds
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: The case for a standardised automotive kernel is not only its scheduling but ease of use and speed to market, and the fact that a standard supports many operating-system vendors, tools and performance tests; nothing in it is specific to vehicles, and it suits any bare-metal problem up to the point where file systems and mass storage push a design toward real-time Linux instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a fully functional real-time operating system that really isn't anything specific to automotive. It should, it should be useful for any kind of bare metal type, uh, problem.
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: A general-purpose cross-vendor RTOS carries a substantially larger footprint than an automotive kernel; it can be trimmed heavily, but that optimisation is left to the user rather than delivered out of the box.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is not small. I mean, it's not, and it's just like, uh, there's a lot of bells and whistles in there too. You can optimize it like crazy, but it's, that's up exercises left to the user.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Team size is a practical deciding criterion for adopting an RTOS framework: at around five people and above, the common vocabulary a shared framework provides is what makes parallel work possible at speed, whereas a solo developer or a very small team gains more by jettisoning that complexity.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I have a team of like 30 people and it's going to be some really big effort, like that's there are 10 people, five people, about five people, I think is where this, this trade-off happens
claims.speaker: CNLohr
claims.episode_title: CH32V003...fun! with CNLohr

claims.claim_text: The price of an RTOS framework is debuggability: a common late-stage failure is a system that almost works while the per-task stack sizes are still being balanced against one another, which is burdensome to resolve.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're having to like balance the size of each one of the stacks and trying to get like, like, oh, but it's, it becomes so burdensome
claims.speaker: CNLohr
claims.episode_title: CH32V003...fun! with CNLohr

claims.claim_text: The presence of a networking stack is the customary marker for moving into RTOS territory, but it is not a requirement: a multiplayer Minecraft server supporting around eight players, with an Ethernet MAC and an SD card for chunk storage, was run on an ATmega328 with roughly 32 kB of flash and 2 kB of RAM.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's got like 32 kilobytes of flash, about two kilobytes of Ram.
claims.speaker: CNLohr
claims.episode_title: CH32V003...fun! with CNLohr

claims.claim_text: A consultancy standardising on an RTOS gave three reasons: starting from an RTOS costs no more development time than a state-machine approach provided it is chosen at the outset rather than switched to mid-project; established boilerplate, templates, drivers and example tasks — a sampling task that queues its results, for instance — save time against writing a state machine each time; and an RTOS shoehorns acceptably into applications where a state machine or bare metal would have been the more natural fit.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you start from RTOS from the start, the time difference for development isn't any more, any less. As long as you start from the start, you don't change halfway through the project because you realize you need an RTOS
claims.speaker: Scott Williams
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: The characteristic defects in RTOS work are stack overflows and heap overflows, but a finite state machine approach produces analogous problems, so they are not by themselves an argument against the kernel.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're getting stack overflows and heap overflows and they're just, you know, working through it constantly. You know, there's always that side, but with a finite state machine approach, you'd still have those similar analogous issues.
claims.speaker: Scott Williams
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: There is a useful distinction between the kernel and the distribution built around it: many projects need only the kernel and nothing more, and the reason they reach for one at all is to move away from a superloop.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's definitely the kernel that many, many people need. And many people don't necessarily need more than that.
claims.speaker: Benjamin Cabe
claims.episode_title: Benjamin Cabé Nose Zephyr

claims.claim_text: Even a Cortex-M0 with about two kilobytes of RAM can run the kernel and use its scheduler to sequence tasks in a timely fashion, though it will not drive a graphical interface; on processors smaller than that a superloop remains the right choice.
claims.quote_verbatim: Cortex M0, like you, you would look at like really, really small, I think like two Ks of RAM
claims.speaker: Benjamin Cabe
claims.episode_title: Benjamin Cabé Nose Zephyr

claims.claim_text: A bare-bones scheduler such as FreeRTOS is well suited to teaching multithreading, because the student starts from the scheduler and adds capability, seeing each layer explicitly.
claims.quote_verbatim: free RTOS absolutely nailed it because it's like a bare bones scheduler. It's so good for teaching multi threading
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Changing Course with Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: Kernel and ecosystem are separate axes: FreeRTOS is a kernel that vendors build ecosystems on top of — Espressif's ESP-IDF layers its parts' capabilities over FreeRTOS — while Zephyr supplies both a kernel with scheduler and a vendor-neutral set of subsystems, so the two are comparable as kernels but reached from different directions.
claims.quote_verbatim: So ESP IDF and Zephyr are both ecosystems. Zephyr and free RTOS are both RTOSs, but then like, it's just kind of which direction you're coming at from them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Changing Course with Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: Some developers replace kernel primitives with their own — writing a private mutex rather than using the supplied one — on the grounds of not trusting code whose internals they have not examined.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wrote my own mutex because I don't trust the mutex on it. It's like, no, I want to know how this stuff works.
claims.speaker: Kevin Cappuccio
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: Event-driven logic written as nested conditionals degenerates quickly, which is the argument for treating everything as a state machine from the outset: a state machine defines the device by a single state at any instant, and that is what makes an environment exactly reproducible for testing and quality assurance.
claims.quote_verbatim: state machines are a beautiful framework for saying at any instant in time, I'm defined by a single state. Once I'm in that state, then I know how to exactly replicate that environment for testing and quality assurance purposes.
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri

claims.claim_text: Threads are not the starting point for a design but a way to express behaviour that is awkward inside a pure state machine — a heartbeat LED that must keep running regardless of the current state is the canonical example, and it belongs in a thread rather than being replicated in every state.
claims.quote_verbatim: using something like a thread is not meant to be the day one starting point usually with something. It's meant to facilitate an ease of implementation that gets trickier to do outside of a pure state machine thing.
claims.speaker: Mark Palmeri
claims.episode_title: Medical Electronics Education with Mark Palmeri
